nodes.question: What are institutions defined as according to North (1991)?
nodes.answer: Institutions are defined as humanly devised constraints that structure political, economic, and social interaction.
nodes.paragraph: 2006 ; Duguma et al. 2014 ; Villamayor-Tomas et al. 2015 ; Runhaar et al. 2018 ). North ( 1991 p. 97) de nes institutions as humanly devised constraints that structure political, economic and socialinteraction. Such interaction between actors is based on formal rules (laws, property rights, policies, and so forth) and informal rules (customs, norms, and so forth) (Ostrom2006 ; Grundmann and Ehlers 2016 ; Spijkerboer et al. 2019 ). In this study, we aim to understand these rules as this allows us to nd out what prevents actors from different sectors from ful Iling integrative potential. The IAD framework by Ostrom ( 2011 ) is a renowned instrument for conducting systematic institutional analysis.It was initially developed in the 1980s as an attempt to structure the elements, categories of factors, and logical interconnections that explain how institutions work(McGinnis 2011a ). Since then, it has evolved signi cantly as well as extended in the form of other frameworks (e.g., the Social-Ecological System (SES) Framework byMcGinnis and Ostrom 2014 ).

nodes.label: Facts
nodes.question: What problem arises from the silos in public administrations?
nodes.answer: The problem that arises from silos in public administrations is coordination difficulties due to the differing perspectives and priorities of each organizational unit, which do not share information with one another.
nodes.paragraph: While the accent in the debate on interactive gover- nance is on the intersectoral, it is equally important to strive for more interaction within the administrative sector itself. The concern with this task is often debatedin terms of challenging the strict separation of different public administrations as silos (Scott & Gong, 2021 ). This leads to coordination problems due to theindividual perspectives and priorities of each organisa- tional unit, which do not share this information (Bogumil & Jann, 2020 ; Hustedt & Radtke, 2024 ). This is particularly evident when a new eld of action such as climate politics emerges, challenging already existing goals and routines across policy areas anddepartments. A shift towards a more co-operative style of action requires reorientation and restructuring steps on allsides (Tuurnas et al., 2023 ) stakeholders and admin- istrators, citizens and politicians. Political organisations and bodies (local councils and elected of cials) as wellas administrations need to open up statehood further to stakeholders from civil society and business. Likewise, civil society organisations cannot just simply regard themselves as a counter-power limiting itself toorganising pressure from below or from outside .

nodes.label: Strategy
nodes.question: What are the three types of strategies defined under the policy mechanisms for solving collective action problems?
nodes.answer: The three types of strategies are rules, incentives, and norms.
nodes.paragraph: While we are interested in what sectors are covered by CAPs, we also seek to better understand the types of strategies employed. Here, we under - stand climate change as a collective action problem (Ostrom 2010 ; Hormio 2023 ) and thus define a strategy typology under policy mechanisms for solving collective action problems: rules, incentives, and norms (Young 2013 ). Each of these three policy tools present opportunities and challenges for city climate action. For instance, when an emissions source falls under a city S jurisdictional powers, new rules can be an efficient path towards rapid GHG reduction. However, environmental regulations can be controversial and easily politicized in the U.S. (Hanna and McDonald 2021 ; Basseches et al. 2022 ), and the majority of community emissions may originate from sectors that cities lack the power to control. In this case, incentives can become a popular option as they help guide but don t overtly control the behavior of private sector and civil society actors. On the other hand, cities require sufficient resources to offer powerful incen - tives, and high emitters must weigh whether an incentive program can adequately cover their costs to reduce emissions.
